title: Entry-Level Wage Impact from AI by 2030
description: Projected change in real wages for entry-level positions (0-2 years experience) across AI-exposed industries by 2030.

sources.title: Entry-Level Job Market Update — Indeed Hiring Lab
sources.excerpt: Entry-level job postings in AI-exposed fields declined 12% YoY. Starting salaries for junior analysts, associates, and coordinators showed early downward pressure.

sources.title: The Wage Divide is Widening Again and AI May Be to Blame
sources.excerpt: Automation pressures are disproportionately suppressing wage gains in lower-paid roles, which is contrary to narratives that AI is mostly impacting high-earning, white-collar jobs.

sources.title: Artificial Intelligence, Automation and Work
sources.excerpt: Theoretical framework for automation's displacement and productivity effects on labor. Automation displaces workers from tasks they previously performed, but productivity gains create new tasks and increase demand for labor.

sources.title: Goldman Sachs economist warns Gen Z tech workers are first on the chopping block
sources.excerpt: Unemployment rate for 20- to 30-year-olds in tech rose nearly 3% since early 2024. Entry-level job postings in the US diminished about 35% since January 2023. Goldman Sachs predicts AI will displace about 6-7% of the total workforce.

sources.title: To prepare young people for the AI workplace, focus on the fundamentals
sources.excerpt: Whether AI destroys jobs or transforms them, young people still need fundamental supports: skill-building, career navigation, and mentorship.

sources.title: Applying AI to Rebuild Middle Class Jobs
sources.excerpt: AI could enable a larger set of workers to perform higher-stakes decision-making tasks currently reserved for elite experts. If used well, AI can help restore the middle-skill, middle-class heart of the US labor market.

sources.title: Entry-Level Jobs Are Vanishing — and AI Is a Big Reason
OECD Youth Employment Outlook 2025
sources.excerpt: Youth (18-24) employment in OECD countries in AI-exposed sectors declined 4.5% YoY. Real starting salaries fell 3-8% across knowledge-work sectors.

sources.title: Usual Weekly Earnings — Workers 16-24
sources.excerpt: Real median weekly earnings for workers aged 16-24 in professional services fell 5.2% from 2023 to 2025.

sources.title: Generative AI and the future of work in America
sources.excerpt: By 2030, activities accounting for up to 30% of hours currently worked could be automated, accelerated by generative AI. Lower-wage workers face up to 14x more occupational transitions than higher-wage counterparts.

sources.title: AI could make half of all entry-level white-collar jobs vanish, Anthropic CEO warns
sources.excerpt: Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei warned that up to 50% of entry-level office jobs could be substantially impacted by AI within the next 2-3 years.

sources.title: Canaries in the Coal Mine? Six Facts about the Recent Employment Effects of AI
sources.publisher: Stanford Digital Economy Lab (Brynjolfsson, Chandar, Chen)
sources.excerpt: We find little difference in annual salary trends by age or exposure quintile, suggesting possible wage stickiness. Labor market adjustments are visible in employment more than in compensation.

sources.title: Bridging Skill Gaps for the Future: New Jobs Creation in the AI Age
sources.excerpt: Emerging evidence that generative AI adoption is reducing entry-level hiring, especially where tasks are automatable rather than complementary to humans.

sources.title: Labor Demand in the Age of Generative AI: Early Evidence from the U.S. Job Posting Data
sources.excerpt: Job postings for high-AI-substitution occupations fell 12% relative to low-substitution roles post-ChatGPT; effect grew from 6% in year one to 18% by year three. Based on 285 million Lightcast job postings.

sources.title: The Labor Market Effects of Generative Artificial Intelligence
sources.publisher: Stanford / World Bank (Hartley, Jolevski, Melo, Moore)
sources.excerpt: 35.9% of US workers used generative AI by December 2025; adoption concentrated among younger, college-educated workers. Small positive wage effects overall.

sources.title: Young workers' employment drops in occupations with high AI exposure
sources.excerpt: Employment share of young workers (20-24) in most AI-exposed occupations fell from 16.4% to 15.5%; decline driven by fewer people transitioning into employment, not layoffs.

sources.title: AI, Productivity, and Labor Markets: A Review of the Empirical Evidence
sources.excerpt: Pressure concentrated in entry-level segments of highly exposed occupations; adjustment happening at the margin through task reallocation.

sources.title: AI and jobs: A review of theory, estimates, and evidence
sources.excerpt: Novice workers benefit more from LLMs in simple tasks but face declining demand across AI-complementary work; digital trace data show substitution in writing and translation.

sources.title: Seniority-Biased Technological Change: Evidence from AI-Adopting Firms
sources.excerpt: Analysis of 62M U.S. resumes: junior employment declined sharply at AI-adopting firms while senior employment was largely unchanged — described as 'seniority-biased technological change.'

sources.title: Task-Specific Technical Change and Comparative Advantage
sources.excerpt: increases the relative productivity of lower-skill workers in tasks and occupations that were previously the territory of higher skilled workers... this lowering of skill-based barriers is the key force reducing inequality

sources.title: AI Exposure and Unemployment Risk
sources.excerpt: Unemployment risk in AI-exposed occupations rose beginning early 2022; graduates with AI-exposed curricula have higher first-job pay and shorter job searches post-ChatGPT.

sources.title: AI is simultaneously aiding and replacing workers, wage data suggest
sources.publisher: Federal Reserve Bank of Dallas (J. Scott Davis)
sources.excerpt: For an occupation with a 0 percent experience premium, increased AI exposure is associated with a 0.28 percentage point reduction in wage growth.

sources.title: The AI Shock and Path Forward: What We Can Learn from the Past to Save Our Future
sources.publisher: Clara Shih (CEO, Salesforce AI) via X
sources.excerpt: new grad hiring in large tech is down over 50% since 2019. For the first time in over decades, recent college grads have a higher unemployment rate than the national average. In addition, the 'underemployment rate' for recent graduates has risen to 42.5% (Q4 2025, New York Federal Reserve).

sources.title: No Country for Young Grads: The Structural Forces That Are Reshaping Entry-Level Employment
sources.excerpt: 52% of the Class of 2023 was underemployed a year after graduating. Entry-level postings in high-AI-exposure occupations fell from 2022 to 2025, while postings requiring 6+ years of experience held steady or rose. Employers reported plans to hire 7.3% more graduates from the Class of 2025; that expectation had been cut to just 0.6%.

sources.title: Looking for the Ladder: Is AI Impacting Entry-Level Jobs?
sources.excerpt: entry-level hiring rates have declined 23 percent compared to pre-pandemic levels, a steeper drop than the 18 percent decline for overall hiring

sources.title: Does Generative AI Narrow Education-Based Productivity Gaps? Evidence from a Randomized Experiment
sources.publisher: NBER (Cruces, Fernández Meijide, Galiani, Gálvez, Lombardi)
sources.excerpt: Without AI, higher-education participants outperformed lower-education participants by 0.548 standard deviations. With AI access, this gap fell to 0.139 standard deviations—closing about 75 percent of the baseline productivity difference.

sources.title: Labor market impacts of AI: A new measure and early evidence
sources.excerpt: Graduate degree holders comprise 17.4% of the most AI-exposed workers vs 4.5% of the unexposed group

sources.title: GenAI and Entry Barriers
sources.excerpt: GenAI modestly changes net wage inequality; entry barriers shift for new workers.

sources.title: Can advanced AI lead to negative economic growth?
sources.excerpt: If broad automation shifts income from un-satiated high-spending (high MPC) workers to the satiated low-spending (low MPC) capital owners, this can trigger a Keynesian demand collapse that contracts the economy

sources.title: Young workers' employment drops in occupations with high AI exposure
sources.excerpt: Employment share for AI-exposed occupations fell from 16.4% (Nov 2022) to 15.5% (Sep 2025). Workers age 22-25 in most AI-exposed occupations experienced 13% employment decline since 2022, driven by fewer workforce entrants rather than layoffs.

sources.title: AI is simultaneously aiding and replacing workers, wage data suggest
sources.excerpt: AI's impact depends on whether it automates or augments. For zero-experience-premium occupations, increased AI exposure is associated with -0.28pp reduction in wage growth. Wages in AI-exposed jobs not uniformly declining.

sources.title: Job Transformation, Specialization, and the Labor Market Effects of AI
sources.excerpt: Low-wage workers gain around 2% on average, whereas wages barely change toward the top (with some outliers).

sources.title: PwC 2025 Global AI Jobs Barometer
sources.excerpt: Employer demand for formal degrees is declining, especially quickly for AI-exposed jobs. The percentage of jobs AI augments that require a degree fell 7 percentage points between 2019 and 2024.

sources.title: Will Wired Belts Become the New Rust Belts? AI and the Emerging Geography of American Job Risk
sources.publisher: Digital Planet, The Fletcher School, Tufts University
sources.excerpt: AI-related job losses are more concentrated in lower-income roles... affecting entry-level roles that are usually repetitive such as administrative, clerical, or data-processing positions

sources.title: AI Narrows Performance Gaps — But Does That Mean It Reduces Inequality?
sources.excerpt: The tasks juniors tend to do—more routine, more codifiable, more text-based—are generally more exposed to AI than what seniors do... the tasks juniors typically perform may be the ones most susceptible to displacement.

sources.title: Expertise
sources.excerpt: A one-standard-deviation decline in the complexity of an occupation's tasks—equivalent to the decline in expertise required by a telephone operator from 1980 to 2018—is linked to an 18% wage decline and a 40% increase in employment per decade.

sources.title: AI Quarterly Pulse Survey Q1 2026
sources.excerpt: 64% say agents have already changed their approach to entry-level hiring

sources.title: How AI may reshape career pathways to better jobs
sources.excerpt: Only 51% of job pathways between Gateway and Destination occupations are not highly exposed to AI.

sources.title: Economists Once Dismissed the A.I. Job Threat, but Not Anymore
sources.excerpt: I really don't know anything a college student can bring to my team that Claude can't do.

sources.title: Goldman Sachs on AI Agents and Labor Market Impact
sources.excerpt: These negative effects fall largely on less experienced workers, widening the entry-level-to-experienced wage gap by 1.3% and the unemployment rate gap by 0.6pp from their pre-pandemic averages.

sources.title: Making Talk Cheap: Generative AI and Labor Market Signaling
sources.excerpt: On Freelancer.com coding jobs, LLM-driven signal degradation redistributes hiring: bottom-quintile workers hired 14% more often, top-quintile hired 19% less often in no-signaling counterfactual.

sources.title: AI's Tech Displacement Effect: Gen Z and the 16,000 Jobs-per-Month Drag
sources.excerpt: The wage gap has similarly deteriorated, with Goldman's regression analysis estimating that a one standard-deviation increase in AI substitution exposure widens the entry-level-to-experienced wage gap by roughly 3.3 percentage points.

sources.title: To save entry-level jobs from AI, look to the medical residency model
sources.excerpt: I've been warning about this risk for over a year; now, the people building the technology are putting timelines on it.

sources.title: Labor Automation Forecasting Hub
sources.publisher: Metaculus / Renaissance Philanthropy / Schultz Family Foundation
sources.excerpt: Overall employment is projected to fall 1.9% by 2030 and fall 3.4% by 2035 due to AI-driven displacement. Unemployment for new 4-year college graduates is projected to more than double to 12% by 2035.

sources.title: You're (not) hired: Artificial intelligence and early career hiring in the Quarterly Workforce Indicators
sources.excerpt: Since ChatGPT's release, it appears that earnings growth has slowed modestly among early career workers in comparison to their peers. However, the decline is small relative to cyclical patterns.
